legend: You wrote a contest where you competed against n$$$n$$$ other participants, and you were given p$$$p$$$ problems to solve.
You solved exactly x$$$x$$$ problems. For each problem i$$$i$$$, you know that it was solved by exactly ki$$$k_i$$$ of your competitors.
You do not know which participants solved which problems. Find the minimum possible number of participants who solved strictly more problems than you.
input: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases t$$$t$$$ (1≤t≤1000$$$1 \le t \le 1000$$$). The description of the test cases follows.

The first line of each test case contains three integers n$$$n$$$, p$$$p$$$, and x$$$x$$$ (1≤n,p≤106$$$1 \le n, p \le 10^6$$$, 0≤x≤p$$$0 \le x \le p$$$) — the number of your competitors, the number of problems, and the number of problems you solved.

The second line of each test case contains p$$$p$$$ integers k1,k2,…,kp$$$k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_p$$$ (0≤ki≤n$$$0 \le k_i \le n$$$), where ki$$$k_i$$$ is the number of other competitors who solved problem i$$$i$$$.
It is guaranteed that the sum of n$$$n$$$ and the sum of p$$$p$$$ over all test cases do not exceed 106$$$10^6$$$.
output: For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum possible number of participants who could have solved strictly more problems than you.
note: In the first test, both of your competitors solved all 4$$$4$$$ problems, but you solved just one, so you are definitely behind both of them.
